vce-psych34-divisions-of-the-nervous-sys: psych34a1-div-1
Which of the following correctly lists the two main divisions of the nervous system?
Central nervous system and peripheral nervous system
Sympathetic nervous system and parasympathetic nervous system
Brain and spinal cord
Somatic nervous system and autonomic nervous system

The nervous system is divided into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (all neural tissue outside the CNS). Somatic/autonomic are the two divisions of the PNS; sympathetic/parasympathetic are the two divisions of the autonomic nervous system.
psych34a1-div-2
The somatic nervous system is best described as the division that
controls involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion
carries sensory information to the CNS and motor commands from the CNS to skeletal muscles
prepares the body for a threat by increasing heart rate
restores the body to a resting state after a threat has passed

The somatic nervous system transmits sensory information to the CNS via sensory (afferent) neurons and motor commands to skeletal muscles via motor (efferent) neurons. Options A, C and D describe the autonomic nervous system and its sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.
psych34a1-div-3
While sitting a VCE exam, Priya notices that her heart is pounding, her pupils have dilated and her digestion has slowed. Which division is most directly responsible for these changes?
Somatic nervous system
Sympathetic nervous system
Central nervous system
Parasympathetic nervous system

Increased heart rate, pupil dilation and inhibited digestion are sympathetic responses that mobilise the body's resources. The parasympathetic nervous system does the opposite, conserving energy and restoring homeostasis.
psych34a1-div-4
Which of the following is a function of the parasympathetic nervous system?
Stimulating the release of adrenaline from the adrenal glands
Dilating the bronchioles to increase oxygen intake
Slowing the heart rate and stimulating digestion
Moving the skeletal muscles of the legs during running
The parasympathetic nervous system conserves energy, slowing heart rate and promoting digestion. A and B are sympathetic responses and D is a function of the somatic nervous system.
psych34a1-div-5
A person suffers damage to the afferent neurons of the spinal nerves in their left arm. The most likely result is that they
can feel touch on the arm but cannot move it
can move the arm but cannot feel touch on it
lose both heart rate regulation and digestion
lose all conscious thought

Afferent (sensory) neurons carry information from the body to the CNS, so damage prevents sensation. Efferent (motor) neurons carry commands to muscles, which remain intact so movement is still possible.
psych34a1-div-6
Distinguish between the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system, giving one component of each. (3 marks)

CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord and processes information and coordinates responses; PNS consists of all the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord (e.g. spinal nerves, cranial nerves) and carries messages between the CNS and the rest of the body; any correct component of each (e.g. brain / somatic nervous system).
psych34a1-div-7
Describe the role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems in the autonomic nervous system, using heart rate as an example. (3 marks)

The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions of internal organs and glands; the sympathetic nervous system arouses the body in response to a threat, e.g. increases heart rate; the parasympathetic nervous system calms the body and returns it to homeostasis, e.g. decreases heart rate back to normal.
psych34a1-div-8

Tom accidentally touches a hot pan, pulls his hand away and then feels his heart racing. Identify which divisions of the nervous system were involved in (a) pulling his hand away and (b) his racing heart. Justify each. (4 marks)

(a) Somatic nervous system; motor neurons carried a command to skeletal muscles in his arm to move it voluntarily/consciously (or by reflex via the spinal cord); sensory neurons carried the pain message to the CNS; (b) Autonomic nervous system, specifically the sympathetic nervous system; the involuntary increase in heart rate is an arousal response to a perceived threat.
vce-psych34-dns-c1
Which of these is NOT an effect of sympathetic nervous system activation?
Increased heart rate
Increased digestion and saliva production
Dilated pupils
Release of glucose from the liver
The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action and slows non-essential processes such as digestion. The parasympathetic nervous system restores 'rest and digest'.
vce-psych34-conscious-and-unconscious-re: psych34a1-con-1
Which of the following is an example of an unconscious response?
Deciding to answer a question in class
Walking to the bus stop while thinking about dinner
Blinking when dust blows into the eye
Planning a route to a friend's house
Unconscious responses occur automatically without awareness or deliberate control, such as blinking and other reflexes. The other options involve awareness and voluntary control.
psych34a1-con-2
A spinal reflex differs from a conscious response because in a spinal reflex
the response is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system only
the response is processed in the spinal cord without needing to reach the brain first
the brain makes a deliberate decision before the muscle moves
only sensory neurons are involved

In a spinal reflex the sensory neuron synapses (often via an interneuron) in the spinal cord, which sends a motor command directly back to the muscle, making the response fast. The brain is informed afterwards but is not required for the response.
psych34a1-con-3
The correct order of neural transmission in a spinal reflex is
sensory neuron, interneuron in spinal cord, motor neuron, effector
interneuron, sensory neuron, brain, motor neuron
sensory neuron, brain, motor neuron, effector
motor neuron, interneuron, sensory neuron, effector

Stimulus detected by receptors, then a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron relays it, a motor neuron carries the command to the effector (muscle). The brain is not part of the reflex pathway itself.
psych34a1-con-4
Which of the following is the best reason a spinal reflex is adaptive?
It uses fewer neurotransmitters than conscious responses
It only occurs in the parasympathetic nervous system
It allows greater conscious control over movement
It produces a response faster than one routed through the brain, reducing potential harm

Bypassing the brain shortens the neural pathway, so the response is quicker and can protect the body from harm. Reflexes are not under conscious control and they do not involve fewer neurotransmitters by definition.
psych34a1-con-5

Ayesha is reading a book when she hears a loud bang. She jerks her head up before she realises what the noise was. She then looks around, deliberately deciding to investigate. The deliberate decision to investigate is best described as
an unconscious response because it involved the spinal cord
a conscious response because it involved awareness and voluntary control
a spinal reflex because it was fast
an autonomic response because it followed a startle
Deliberately choosing to investigate involves awareness and voluntary decision making, which is a conscious response involving the brain. The initial jerk was the unconscious startle response.
psych34a1-con-6
Define a spinal reflex and explain why it can occur without conscious awareness. (3 marks)

A spinal reflex is an unconscious, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus; the sensory neuron sends the message to the spinal cord where it is passed via an interneuron to a motor neuron that triggers the muscle; the brain is not required to process the message, so it occurs before awareness of the stimulus is registered.
psych34a1-con-7
Compare conscious and unconscious responses in terms of speed and the role of the brain, using one example of each. (4 marks)

Conscious responses involve awareness and voluntary control with the brain processing information, so are slower, e.g. deciding to catch a ball; unconscious responses occur automatically without awareness or brain-based decision making, so are usually faster, e.g. withdrawing a hand from a sharp object via spinal reflex; correct example of each given; comparison of both speed and brain involvement.
psych34a1-con-8

A nurse taps just below Jamal's kneecap and his lower leg kicks out. Identify the type of response, describe the pathway of the neural message, and explain why Jamal cannot stop the kick by deciding not to. (4 marks)

Unconscious spinal reflex; sensory neuron detects the stretch and sends a message to the spinal cord, then via an interneuron to a motor neuron that causes the thigh muscle to contract; the response is processed at the spinal cord without the brain deciding; it is involuntary and occurs too quickly for conscious control to intervene.
vce-psych34-cu-c1
Someone touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before they feel pain. The best explanation is that:
The brain sends the withdrawal message before it has processed the pain, so the movement comes first
Motor neurons in the hand detect the heat directly and contract the arm muscles
Interneurons in the spinal cord link sensory and motor neurons, so the response starts before the pain message reaches the brain
The autonomic nervous system takes over the arm's skeletal muscles in an emergency
In a spinal reflex the response is organised in the spinal cord, so movement begins before the pain signal reaches the somatosensory cortex and is perceived.
vce-psych34-neurotransmitters-and-neurom: psych34a1-ntm-1
Which of the following best describes the role of an excitatory neurotransmitter?
It stops the presynaptic neuron from producing action potentials
It decreases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire
It increases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire
It destroys the postsynaptic receptor sites
Excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate bind to receptors and make the postsynaptic neuron more likely to fire an action potential. Inhibitory neurotransmitters, such as GABA, do the opposite.
psych34a1-ntm-2
Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system?
GABA
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Glutamate
GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter and reduces the likelihood the postsynaptic neuron fires. Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter.
psych34a1-ntm-3
Neuromodulators differ from neurotransmitters because neuromodulators
are produced only by the gut
are only released by the peripheral nervous system
alter the effect of neurotransmitters on the postsynaptic neuron, often across many neurons
always directly cause the postsynaptic neuron to fire

Neuromodulators influence the transmission of neural information by adjusting the strength or effect of neurotransmitters, often acting on groups of neurons. Neurotransmitters directly transmit signals across a single synapse, either exciting or inhibiting the postsynaptic neuron.
psych34a1-ntm-4
In the synapse, after a neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic neuron it
crosses the synaptic gap and binds to receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron
travels back along the axon of the presynaptic neuron
is converted to an electrical impulse in the synaptic gap
binds to receptors on the presynaptic vesicles

Neurotransmitters are released from vesicles at the axon terminal, diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to complementary receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron. The signal is chemical across the gap, not electrical.
psych34a1-ntm-5
A drug blocks GABA from binding to its receptors on postsynaptic neurons in a region of the brain. The most likely effect is
increased inhibition of those neurons
decreased likelihood that the neurons will be excited
increased likelihood that the neurons will fire
no change in neural activity
GABA is inhibitory, so blocking it removes inhibition and the neurons become more likely to fire. Option A is the opposite of the effect.
psych34a1-ntm-6
Describe the difference between an excitatory neurotransmitter and an inhibitory neurotransmitter, naming one example of each. (3 marks)

Excitatory neurotransmitters increase the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire an action potential, e.g. glutamate; inhibitory neurotransmitters decrease the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire, e.g. GABA; both bind to receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron.
psych34a1-ntm-7
Outline the process of neurotransmission at a chemical synapse. (4 marks)

An action potential arrives at the axon terminal of the presynaptic neuron; vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synaptic gap; neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to complementary receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron; this has an excitatory or inhibitory effect on the postsynaptic neuron, making it more or less likely to fire.
psych34a1-ntm-8
Dopamine is described as a neuromodulator. Explain how a neuromodulator differs in its effect from a neurotransmitter such as glutamate. (3 marks)

Glutamate is a neurotransmitter that directly acts at the synapse to excite the postsynaptic neuron; a neuromodulator such as dopamine does not by itself simply transmit the signal but influences/regulates the effect of neurotransmitters; it can change the sensitivity or responsiveness of neurons, often over many neurons at once, thereby adjusting the strength of neural communication.
vce-psych34-nt-c1
A drug blocks GABA receptors on post-synaptic neurons. The most likely effect is:
Deep relaxation and sleepiness, as with benzodiazepines
Less glutamate release, so neurons fire less readily
Improved memory consolidation through stronger LTP
More neural excitation, such as anxiety or even seizures
GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Blocking its receptors removes the 'brake', so neurons fire more readily.
vce-psych34-synaptic-plasticity-and-long: psych34a1-ltp-1
Synaptic plasticity refers to
the permanent loss of neurons through ageing
the ability of synapses to change in strength in response to activity
the speed at which an action potential travels along an axon
the production of new neurons in the gut
Synaptic plasticity is the ability of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time in response to their activity, underlying learning and memory. It is not about neuron loss or axon conduction speed.
psych34a1-ltp-2
Long-term potentiation (LTP) is best described as
the death of unused neurons
the temporary storage of information in short-term memory
a long-lasting weakening of synaptic connections
a long-lasting strengthening of synaptic connections following repeated stimulation

LTP is a long-lasting strengthening of synaptic transmission following repeated or intense stimulation, and is a mechanism for learning and memory. Long-term depression (LTD) is the long-lasting weakening.
psych34a1-ltp-3
Which neurotransmitter plays a key role in LTP?
GABA
Glutamate
Cortisol
Adrenaline

Glutamate released from the presynaptic neuron binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron and is central to LTP, which strengthens the synapse. GABA is inhibitory and cortisol and adrenaline are hormones.
psych34a1-ltp-4
Long-term depression (LTD) results in
an increase in the number of action potentials produced by the postsynaptic neuron
a stronger synaptic connection due to frequent firing
a weaker synaptic connection due to infrequent or low-level stimulation
the formation of new neurotransmitters
LTD is a long-lasting decrease in the strength of synaptic transmission, which helps remove unused connections. It is the opposite of LTP, which is a strengthening.
psych34a1-ltp-5
A student practises vocabulary using spaced repetition, and over several weeks recalls the words more easily. Which neural change is the most likely contributor?
Long-term potentiation of the relevant synapses
A decrease in glutamate release from the relevant neurons
Increased GABA activity at the relevant synapses
Long-term depression of the relevant synapses

Repeated activation of the same neural pathway strengthens its synapses through LTP, making transmission more efficient and supporting memory. LTD and increased GABA would weaken or inhibit the pathway.
psych34a1-ltp-6
Define long-term potentiation and state its relevance to learning. (3 marks)

LTP is a long-lasting increase in the strength of synaptic transmission between neurons following repeated stimulation; it makes it easier for the presynaptic neuron to trigger the postsynaptic neuron; it is a cellular basis of learning and memory because strengthened pathways support retention of new information.
psych34a1-ltp-7
Explain how the neurotransmitter glutamate contributes to long-term potentiation. (3 marks)

Glutamate is released from the presynaptic neuron into the synapse and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron; repeated stimulation leads to more/stronger receptor activity (e.g. more receptors on the postsynaptic membrane) so the postsynaptic neuron responds more strongly; this strengthens the synapse, producing LTP.
psych34a1-ltp-8
Contrast long-term potentiation and long-term depression, and explain why both are important for the functioning of neural circuits. (4 marks)

LTP strengthens synaptic connections after high-frequency/repeated activity; LTD weakens synaptic connections after low-frequency/infrequent activity; LTP supports the formation and consolidation of memories; LTD removes or weakens unused or unnecessary connections, which refines neural circuits and allows flexibility in learning.
vce-psych34-sp-c1
A student practises violin every day for a year, then stops for several months. Which best describes the changes at the synapses involved?
Long-term depression while practising, then long-term potentiation after stopping
Only pruning, because adults do not form new connections
No change, because the skill is stored in muscle memory
Long-term potentiation while practising, then long-term depression after stopping
Repeated stimulation strengthens synaptic connections (LTP). With little use, connections weaken (LTD), which is why skills fade without practice.
vce-psych34-stress-responses-and-the-gas: psych34a1-gas-1
Stress is best defined as
a type of mental disorder
a response that only occurs with negative events
an event that always leads to illness
a state of threat or challenge that causes a physiological and psychological response
Stress is a psychological and physiological response to a perceived demand or threat, which can be positive or negative. It is not a disorder and it can involve both distress and eustress.
psych34a1-gas-2
Eustress differs from distress in that eustress
has no physiological effects
is a negative stress response that damages health
is a positive form of stress that can motivate and enhance performance
occurs only in the exhaustion stage of the GAS
Eustress is a positive form of stress, often experienced as motivation or excitement, such as before a sporting final. Distress is the negative form that causes anxiety or damages wellbeing.
psych34a1-gas-3
In the fight-flight-freeze response, which hormone released by the adrenal medulla increases heart rate and blood flow to muscles?
Adrenaline
Insulin
Melatonin
Cortisol

Adrenaline (released by the adrenal medulla, triggered by the sympathetic nervous system) raises heart rate and mobilises energy. Cortisol is released from the adrenal cortex and supports longer-term stress responses.
psych34a1-gas-4
According to Selye's general adaptation syndrome (GAS), in which stage does the body's resistance to the stressor fall below normal and the person becomes susceptible to illness?
Resistance
Exhaustion
Alarm reaction: shock phase
Alarm reaction: counter-shock phase

In exhaustion, prolonged exposure depletes the body's resources, so resistance falls and illness becomes more likely. In resistance the body copes with elevated physiological arousal, and the alarm stage is the initial reaction.
psych34a1-gas-5
During the resistance stage of the GAS, the body typically
shows a sharp drop in blood pressure and body temperature
maintains elevated cortisol levels while attempting to cope with the stressor
returns fully to homeostasis because the stressor has been removed
activates the freeze response only

In resistance the body continues to cope with the ongoing stressor with elevated physiological arousal (including cortisol), though outwardly it may seem normal. The shock phase of alarm involves the initial drop in resistance.
psych34a1-gas-6
Describe the alarm reaction stage of the general adaptation syndrome, including its two phases. (3 marks)

Alarm reaction is the initial response to a stressor; shock phase: the body's resistance temporarily drops (e.g. decreased heart rate and blood pressure) as it perceives the stressor; counter-shock phase: the sympathetic nervous system is activated, adrenaline and cortisol are released, increasing heart rate and mobilising energy for fight-flight-freeze.
psych34a1-gas-7
Explain how the role of cortisol differs from the role of adrenaline in the stress response. (3 marks)

Adrenaline is released rapidly by the adrenal medulla and produces immediate effects such as increased heart rate and blood flow; cortisol is released more slowly by the adrenal cortex via the HPA axis and acts over a longer period, releasing glucose and maintaining energy supply; prolonged high cortisol is associated with the resistance and exhaustion stages and negative health effects.
psych34a1-gas-8

Dana has spent eight months caring for a sick relative, working full time and sleeping poorly. She has recently developed frequent colds and feels constantly drained. Use the GAS to explain her symptoms. (4 marks)

Her prolonged stress corresponds to the resistance stage, where she has been coping with elevated physiological arousal; over time her bodily resources were depleted so she has entered the exhaustion stage; in exhaustion, resistance to stress falls below normal and the immune system is weakened, explaining the frequent colds; feeling drained reflects depleted energy resources from sustained cortisol and arousal.
vce-psych34-gas-c1
In Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome, why is a person in the resistance stage more likely to catch a cold?
Resistance falls below normal throughout this stage
High cortisol levels over a long period suppress the immune system
The sympathetic nervous system is switched off
Adrenaline levels are at their lowest
Cortisol keeps resistance to the original stressor above normal, but prolonged release weakens immune function, making new illnesses more likely.
vce-psych34-transactional-model-of-stres: psych34a1-tmc-1
The transactional model of stress and coping was developed by
Skinner
Selye
Lazarus and Folkman
Bandura
The transactional model of stress and coping was proposed by Lazarus and Folkman. Selye developed the GAS, Bandura observational learning and Skinner operant conditioning.
psych34a1-tmc-2
According to the transactional model, stress is best seen as
a transaction between the individual and the environment, depending on appraisal
a purely physiological response
an unavoidable outcome of any demand
an objective property of an event that affects everyone equally

In the transactional model, stress arises from the interaction between a person and their environment and depends on how the person appraises the situation and their ability to cope. Different people can appraise the same event differently.
psych34a1-tmc-3
In primary appraisal, a person decides whether an event is
a physiological or psychological demand
controllable or uncontrollable
irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful
approach or avoidance coping
Primary appraisal evaluates the event itself as irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful (harm/loss, threat or challenge). Secondary appraisal then evaluates coping resources and options.
psych34a1-tmc-4
Secondary appraisal involves
deciding whether an event is relevant to wellbeing
evaluating whether one has the resources and abilities to cope with the event
the body's physiological reaction in the alarm stage
stopping to think about the event after it has passed
Secondary appraisal is the assessment of one's coping resources and options for dealing with the stressor. Option A describes primary appraisal.
psych34a1-tmc-5

Two students receive identical news that their exam will be moved forward by a week. Mia views it as a challenge she can prepare for; Leo views it as a threat he cannot handle. According to the transactional model, the difference is best explained by their
different primary and secondary appraisals
differences in their parasympathetic response
levels of cortisol before the news
differences in the event itself

The model emphasises that stress depends on appraisal: Mia appraised the event as a challenge and judged she had resources to cope, while Leo appraised it as a threat with inadequate resources. The event itself was identical.
psych34a1-tmc-6
Distinguish between primary appraisal and secondary appraisal in the transactional model of stress and coping. (3 marks)

Primary appraisal is the initial evaluation of an event as irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful; secondary appraisal is the evaluation of one's ability and resources to cope with the event; if resources are judged inadequate the situation is more likely to be experienced as stressful.
psych34a1-tmc-7

Hannah has just been told she must give a presentation to her whole year level next week. She feels nervous, but thinks she has presented well before and has time to practise. Using the transactional model, describe her primary and secondary appraisal. (4 marks)

Primary appraisal: she judges the presentation as stressful (a challenge/threat) because it is relevant to her wellbeing; secondary appraisal: she assesses her coping resources positively (past experience, time to practise); because she believes she can cope, she is likely to experience it as a challenge, leading to lower stress; coping strategies are chosen in response.
psych34a1-tmc-8
Explain one strength and one limitation of the transactional model of stress and coping. (3 marks)

Strength: it recognises individual differences in appraisal so explains why the same event is stressful for one person but not another (and links to coping choices); limitation: it focuses on cognitive appraisal and may underplay physiological aspects of stress or the role of objective stressor severity; appraisal is difficult to measure objectively and relies on self-report.
vce-psych34-tm-c1
Mia sees a new job as a chance to grow, although she knows it will be demanding. She then decides her friends and her mentor can help her manage it. Her two appraisals are:
Primary appraisal: benign-positive; secondary appraisal: threat
Primary appraisal: irrelevant; secondary appraisal: challenge
Primary appraisal: harm/loss; secondary appraisal: benign-positive
Primary appraisal: stressful (challenge); secondary appraisal: evaluating her coping resources
A challenge appraisal is stressful but focuses on potential gain. Secondary appraisal asks: what resources do I have to cope?
vce-psych34-gut-brain-axis: psych34a1-gba-1
The gut-brain axis refers to
the bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system
the one-way flow of signals from the brain to the stomach
the transfer of food from the stomach to the brain
a neural pathway connecting the brain and the gut only through the spinal cord
The gut-brain axis is the bidirectional communication between the gut (including its microbiota and enteric nervous system) and the brain via neural, hormonal and immune pathways.
psych34a1-gba-2
The enteric nervous system is
found only in the spinal cord
a network of neurons embedded in the walls of the gastrointestinal tract
the part of the brain that regulates hunger only
a division of the somatic nervous system
The enteric nervous system is a network of neurons lining the gastrointestinal tract that regulates digestion and communicates with the CNS, often called the 'second brain'.
psych34a1-gba-3
The vagus nerve contributes to the gut-brain axis by
carrying signals between the gut and the brain in both directions
storing neurotransmitters in the stomach
controlling skeletal muscle movement
producing the gut microbiota
The vagus nerve is a major pathway for bidirectional communication between the gut and brainstem. It does not produce microbiota.
psych34a1-gba-4
Which statement about gut microbiota and mental health is best supported by the gut-brain axis?
Gut microbiota are only affected by diet and have no effect on the brain
Gut microbiota only exist in the central nervous system
Gut microbiota are unrelated to the nervous system
Gut microbiota can influence the production of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, which may affect mood and stress responses
Gut microbiota influence the production and regulation of neurotransmitters (a large proportion of serotonin is produced in the gut) and can affect stress responses and mood via the gut-brain axis.
psych34a1-gba-5
A researcher finds that stressed participants experience more digestive discomfort than non-stressed participants. This finding is most consistent with
signals from the brain affecting gut function via the gut-brain axis
the gut being unable to communicate with the brain
the enteric nervous system being unrelated to stress
the parasympathetic nervous system being fully activated
Stress signals travel from the brain to the gut (e.g. via the sympathetic nervous system and HPA axis), altering digestion and gut function. This demonstrates the brain-to-gut direction of the axis.
psych34a1-gba-6
Explain what is meant by the statement that communication in the gut-brain axis is 'bidirectional'. (2 marks)

Signals travel from the brain to the gut (e.g. stress altering digestion); and signals also travel from the gut to the brain (e.g. gut microbiota and gut-produced chemicals influencing mood and stress response).
psych34a1-gba-7
Describe the role of gut microbiota in the gut-brain axis. (3 marks)

Gut microbiota are the community of microorganisms living in the gut; they influence the production of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and other signalling chemicals; these signals reach the brain via the vagus nerve, immune and hormonal pathways and so can influence mood, stress responses and behaviour.
psych34a1-gba-8

A study gives one group of volunteers a probiotic and another group a placebo for four weeks. The probiotic group reports lower stress and anxiety scores. Use the gut-brain axis to explain this result and identify one limitation in concluding causation. (4 marks)

Probiotics may alter the composition of gut microbiota, changing production of neurotransmitters (e.g. serotonin) and signalling to the brain via the vagus nerve, which could reduce stress and anxiety; limitation: stress and anxiety were self-reported so subject to bias (or small sample, other lifestyle variables not controlled, placebo effect); a link is not enough to prove the probiotic alone caused the change, and the mechanism was not measured directly.
vce-psych34-gb-c1
Chronic stress changes a person's gut microbiota, and the changed microbiota then worsens their mood. This best illustrates that the gut–brain axis is:
One-directional, from the gut to the brain only
Bidirectional: the brain affects the gut and the gut affects the brain
Controlled only by the somatic nervous system
Unrelated to the vagus nerve
The CNS and the enteric nervous system communicate both ways, including via the vagus nerve and chemicals produced by gut microbes.
vce-psych34-coping-strategies-and-flexib: psych34a1-cop-1
Approach coping strategies are
unconscious responses such as reflexes
strategies that aim to avoid or ignore the stressor
strategies that aim to confront and deal directly with the stressor
strategies that always reduce stress in every context
Approach strategies involve confronting the stressor directly, such as problem solving or seeking support. Avoidance strategies involve evading or ignoring the stressor.
psych34a1-cop-2
Which of the following is an example of an avoidance coping strategy?
Talking to a teacher about difficulties with a subject
Spending hours playing video games to avoid thinking about an upcoming exam
Breaking a large assignment into smaller tasks
Making a study timetable for an upcoming exam
Using distraction to avoid thinking about the stressor is avoidance coping. The other options are approach strategies that confront the stressor directly.
psych34a1-cop-3
Coping flexibility is best defined as
the ability to avoid stress completely
always using the same coping strategy regardless of the situation
the ability to adapt coping strategies to suit the demands of different stressful situations
avoiding all stressful situations
Coping flexibility is the ability to change or adapt coping strategies depending on the context and the effectiveness of the strategy currently being used.
psych34a1-cop-4
A strategy is considered 'context-specific' in its effectiveness when
it works equally well in all situations
its effectiveness depends on the nature of the stressor and the situation
it is always an avoidance strategy
it is only effective for people with high stress levels

Context-specific effectiveness means that a coping strategy may be useful in some situations but not others. For example, avoidance may help temporarily with an uncontrollable stressor but not with an upcoming deadline.
psych34a1-cop-5

Callum is anxious about a looming deadline and tries distraction by watching movies, but his anxiety increases as the deadline nears. He then makes a plan, breaks the task into steps and starts working. This change in approach is best described as
primary appraisal
a spinal reflex
coping inflexibility
coping flexibility
Callum recognised the ineffective avoidance strategy and shifted to an approach strategy better suited to the situation, demonstrating coping flexibility.
psych34a1-cop-6
Distinguish between approach and avoidance coping strategies, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Approach coping involves confronting or dealing directly with the stressor, e.g. making a plan or seeking social support; avoidance coping involves evading, ignoring or withdrawing from the stressor, e.g. distraction or procrastinating; correct example of each.
psych34a1-cop-7
Explain why the effectiveness of a coping strategy is described as context-specific. Use an example. (3 marks)

A coping strategy's effectiveness depends on the situation and the stressor; a strategy may be adaptive in one context and maladaptive in another; example: avoidance such as distraction may help short-term with an uncontrollable situation (e.g. waiting for medical results) but be ineffective for a controllable one (e.g. an upcoming assignment) where an approach strategy such as planning is more effective.
psych34a1-cop-8
Describe coping flexibility and explain why it may be beneficial for a person's wellbeing. (3 marks)

Coping flexibility is the ability to adapt or switch coping strategies according to the changing demands of the stressor/context and whether the current strategy is working; it is beneficial because it allows the person to choose the most appropriate strategy, e.g. approach when the stressor is controllable and avoidance when it is not; this leads to more effective stress management and better psychological wellbeing.
vce-psych34-cf-c1
Which example best shows coping flexibility?
A student who always goes for a run to cope, whatever the stressor happens to be
A student who avoids thinking about an exam until the night before, to stay calm
A student who keeps using the same strategy because it worked well last year
A student who finds re-reading notes isn't working switches to practice exams and asking a teacher
Coping flexibility means recognising when a strategy is ineffective and changing to one that suits the situation (context-specific effectiveness).
vce-psych34-classical-conditioning: psych34a1-cc-1
Classical conditioning was first systematically investigated by
Bandura
Pavlov
Lazarus
Skinner
Ivan Pavlov studied classical conditioning in dogs, showing they could be conditioned to salivate to a neutral stimulus. Skinner studied operant conditioning and Bandura observational learning.
psych34a1-cc-2
In classical conditioning, the unconditioned response (UCR) is
the consequence that follows a behaviour
a learned response to the conditioned stimulus
an automatic response to the unconditioned stimulus that does not need to be learned
the neutral stimulus before conditioning
The UCR is a naturally occurring, automatic response to the unconditioned stimulus (UCS). The learned response to the conditioned stimulus is the conditioned response (CR).
psych34a1-cc-3
Marcus eats a particular brand of chips and later gets food poisoning from a different meal. Now, the smell of the chips makes him feel nauseous. In this scenario the conditioned stimulus is
the nausea felt after food poisoning
the smell of the chips
the other meal
the food poisoning

Before conditioning the chips were a neutral stimulus. After being paired with the UCS (food poisoning), the chips became a CS that elicits the CR (nausea). The food poisoning is the UCS and the nausea in response to it is the UCR.
psych34a1-cc-4
Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when
the CS is presented before the UCS
the organism responds to stimuli similar to the CS
the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS, so the CR gradually weakens and disappears
the CR suddenly reappears after a rest period

Extinction is the gradual weakening and disappearance of the CR when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS. Reappearance after a rest is spontaneous recovery; responding to similar stimuli is generalisation.
psych34a1-cc-5
A child who was frightened by a large brown dog now becomes fearful when they see any large dog. This is an example of
stimulus discrimination
extinction
spontaneous recovery
stimulus generalisation
Stimulus generalisation occurs when stimuli similar to the original CS also elicit the CR. Discrimination would be responding only to the specific CS and not to similar ones.
psych34a1-cc-6

Identify the NS, UCS, UCR, CS and CR in the following scenario: A student always hears the school bell just before being given a free lunch tray, which makes her salivate. After many weeks, the bell alone makes her salivate. (5 marks)
NS (before conditioning): the school bell; UCS: the free lunch/food; UCR: salivation in response to the food; CS (after conditioning): the school bell; CR: salivation in response to the bell alone.
psych34a1-cc-7
Describe the process of acquisition in classical conditioning, including the role of timing between the stimuli. (3 marks)

Acquisition is the stage during which the association between the NS and UCS is formed; the NS is repeatedly paired with the UCS; learning is most effective when the NS is presented just before/slightly before the UCS (contiguity); once the NS elicits the response alone it becomes the CS and the response becomes the CR.
psych34a1-cc-8

A dog has been conditioned to salivate to a tone. After extinction, the tone is presented again following a rest period and the dog salivates slightly. Name this phenomenon and explain what it suggests about extinction. (3 marks)

Spontaneous recovery; the reappearance of a previously extinguished CR after a rest period without further pairing; suggests extinction does not completely erase the learned association, it is suppressed, and the CR is usually weaker than at acquisition.
vce-psych34-cc-c1
Leo eats sushi that contains bacteria and is violently ill. Afterwards the smell of sushi makes him nauseous. In this example the unconditioned stimulus (UCS) is:
The smell of sushi
Nausea
The restaurant
The bacteria that made him ill
The bacteria naturally cause illness (UCS → UCR: nausea). Sushi was a neutral stimulus that, after pairing, became the CS, producing nausea as a CR.
vce-psych34-operant-conditioning: Operant conditioning is best described as learning in which
an association is formed between two stimuli
behaviour is shaped by its consequences
behaviour is acquired by observing others
reflexes are changed by repeated stimulus
In operant conditioning, behaviour is influenced by its consequences (reinforcement and punishment). Option A describes classical conditioning and option C observational learning.
In the three-phase model of operant conditioning, the three phases are

The three-phase model consists of antecedent (the stimulus before the behaviour), behaviour (the response) and consequence (what follows the behaviour). The other options relate to classical conditioning and observational learning.
A parent stops nagging a teenager once they have finished their homework. The teenager is now more likely to complete their homework in the future. This is an example of

Negative reinforcement is the removal of an unpleasant stimulus (nagging) following a behaviour, which increases the likelihood of the behaviour recurring. Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus.
A child's pocket money is taken away after they hit their sibling. The aim is to decrease hitting. This is best classified as
Negative punishment is the removal of a desirable stimulus (pocket money) following a behaviour to decrease it. Positive punishment would add an unpleasant stimulus.
A coach praises a swimmer every time she achieves a personal best. Which of the following is the antecedent in the three-phase model?
The swimming race or training session in which the swimmer attempts a personal best
The antecedent is the stimulus or situation that occurs before the behaviour (the race/training). The behaviour is the swim and the praise is the consequence (a positive reinforcer).

Using the three-phase model of operant conditioning, analyse the following: A toddler is given a sticker each time she puts her toys away after play time. Identify the antecedent, behaviour and consequence and state the effect on behaviour. (4 marks)

Antecedent: play time finishes (or being asked to tidy up); behaviour: she puts her toys away; consequence: she receives a sticker (positive reinforcement); effect: the behaviour is more likely to be repeated in the future.
Distinguish between positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement, giving an example of each. (4 marks)

Positive reinforcement is the addition of a pleasant stimulus after a behaviour, increasing the likelihood of the behaviour, e.g. a dog receives a treat for sitting; negative reinforcement is the removal of an unpleasant stimulus after a behaviour, also increasing the likelihood of the behaviour, e.g. taking painkillers to remove a headache; both increase behaviour, differing in whether a stimulus is added or removed.

A teacher gives detention (positive punishment) to a student who keeps arriving late, but the lateness continues. Suggest two reasons why the punishment may not be effective and one alternative using operant conditioning. (3 marks)

Reasons (any two): punishment may not be delivered consistently or immediately after the behaviour; the student may find detention not aversive or may gain attention from it (which could reinforce the behaviour); punishment shows what not to do rather than what to do; alternative: use positive reinforcement, e.g. praise or reward for arriving on time.
A car beeps until the driver fastens their seatbelt, and the driver now buckles up straight away. The behaviour has been strengthened by:
Removing an unpleasant stimulus (the beeping) makes the behaviour more likely. Punishment always makes behaviour less likely.
vce-psych34-observational-learning: Observational learning was extensively studied by
Albert Bandura investigated observational learning, notably through the Bobo doll experiments. Pavlov studied classical conditioning and Skinner operant conditioning.
According to Bandura, which of the following is the correct order of the stages of observational learning?

The stages in the VCE study design are attention, retention, reproduction, motivation and reinforcement. The observer must first attend to the model and store the information before being able to reproduce the behaviour.
In observational learning, a model is
the reinforcement that follows the behaviour
the memory of the observed behaviour
the person who is observed and whose behaviour is imitated
A model is the person whose behaviour is observed and potentially imitated. The learner is the observer.
A child sees an older cousin being praised for sharing toys. Later, the child shares their own toys. The child's behaviour is best explained by
Vicarious reinforcement occurs when an observer sees a model being rewarded, which increases the likelihood that the observer will imitate the behaviour. No direct reward was given to the child.
Which of the following demonstrates the 'retention' stage of observational learning?
A trainee watches a chef closely as she chops vegetables
A trainee remembers the chef's technique when practising later that evening
A trainee attempts to chop vegetables in the same way as the chef
A trainee is praised by the chef for improving
Retention is storing the observed behaviour in memory so it can be recalled later. Option A is attention, option C is reproduction and option D is reinforcement.
Outline the five stages of observational learning as proposed by Bandura. (5 marks)

Attention: the observer pays attention to the model's behaviour; retention: the observer stores the behaviour in memory; reproduction: the observer is physically able to replicate the behaviour; motivation: the observer has a reason or desire to perform the behaviour; reinforcement: the observer is reinforced (directly or vicariously) or expects reinforcement, making the behaviour more likely to be repeated.
Describe how Bandura's Bobo doll experiment demonstrated observational learning. (3 marks)

Children observed an adult model behaving aggressively toward an inflatable Bobo doll (or non-aggressively in a control condition); when later placed in a room with the doll, children who had seen aggression imitated the same aggressive acts; this showed behaviour can be learned by observation without direct reinforcement.

Lena watches an online tutorial in which a baker is applauded for decorating a cake with a new piping technique. Lena wants to copy the technique, but her first attempt is messy. Explain how the stages of attention and reproduction apply, and why reproduction may have failed. (4 marks)

Attention: Lena watched and focused on the baker's technique; reproduction: Lena tries to physically replicate the behaviour from memory; reproduction may have failed because she lacks the motor skill or practice, or her retention of the details was incomplete; with more practice and feedback her reproduction can improve.
A child watches a cooking show closely, remembers every step and wants to cook, but cannot reach the bench or use the knife safely. Which stage of observational learning is not met?
Reproduction requires the physical and mental ability to perform the behaviour. The child attended, retained and was motivated.
vce-psych34-aboriginal-and-torres-strait: psych34a2-atsi-1
Which statement best describes the role of Country in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning and memory?
Learning occurs only inside formal classrooms and is later applied to Country
Country is used only to teach practical survival skills and not stories or law
Country is a backdrop that has little influence on what is learnt
Knowledge is closely tied to place, so features of the land act as cues that hold and help recall cultural knowledge
Knowledge, stories and law are linked to specific places, so landscape features act as memory cues. A is wrong because Country is central, not incidental.
psych34a2-atsi-2

An Elder guides a group of young people along a route, telling a story and singing at each landmark. Later the young people can recount the route and the associated knowledge. This is best described as a use of
songlines
the method of loci applied to a written map
rote rehearsal of unrelated lists
a Western standardised test
Songlines link story, song and landscape so that knowledge is stored and recalled in sequence. The method of loci is a Western mnemonic term; here the cultural practice is songlines.
psych34a2-atsi-3
Which of the following is a common feature of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning?
Learning is individual and competitive, with a focus on personal achievement
Learning is delivered only by written texts
Learning is community-based, often through observation, practice and storytelling with kin and Elders
Learning is limited to young children
Community-based, relational learning through observation, imitation, practice and stories is a key feature. Option A reflects an individualistic approach, not a typical feature of these approaches.
psych34a2-atsi-4
Why are stories, art, dance and song particularly effective for passing on cultural knowledge across generations?
They link information to meaningful, emotional, multisensory experiences that are shared and repeated, which supports memory
They are quicker to learn than any written record
They make knowledge more private to each individual
They remove the need for any social interaction
Multisensory, shared, repeated and meaningful experiences strengthen encoding and retrieval. D is incorrect: the knowledge is communal.
psych34a2-atsi-5
Kinship systems in many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities are relevant to learning because they
are separate from cultural knowledge
decide who is allowed to attend school
define relationships and responsibilities, including who teaches particular knowledge and to whom
replace the need for oral traditions
Kinship specifies relationships and roles, including who holds and passes on certain knowledge. A is not a function of kinship systems in this context.
psych34a2-atsi-6
Describe one way in which connection to Country supports learning and memory in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures. (2 marks)

1 mark for a feature of Country-based learning (e.g. knowledge, story or law is linked to specific places/landmarks; songlines); 1 mark for explaining how it supports memory (e.g. landmarks act as retrieval cues, linking information to place and sequence makes it easier to recall, learning in context).
psych34a2-atsi-7

A teacher in a Victorian school wants to include learning approaches used by local Aboriginal communities in a unit on the history of the local area. Suggest two strategies consistent with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning and explain how each could aid students' learning. (4 marks)

Any two strategies, each with an explanation, 1 mark for strategy and 1 mark for explanation: invite a local Elder or community member to share stories (learning from Elders in a community context, knowledge held in oral stories, relevant and respectful); take learning outdoors onto Country (links knowledge to place, landmarks as retrieval cues, multisensory); use storytelling, art, song or dance to represent events (multisensory, emotional, shared and repeated); learning through observation and practice in small groups (collaborative, social learning).
psych34a2-atsi-8
Explain, with reference to memory, why oral traditions and songlines have been able to preserve detailed knowledge over thousands of years. (3 marks)

Information is encoded in song, story and rhythm, which gives structure and aids retrieval; the knowledge is linked to physical landmarks on Country, which act as cues and give a sequence; it is repeated, rehearsed and passed on through the community and Elders with shared responsibility, so it is maintained and checked across generations (also acceptable: multisensory and emotional meaning).
vce-psych34-at-c1
Which statement best describes the role of Country in many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning?
Country is the place where formal written tests are held at the end of each stage of learning
Learning happens mainly by reading texts silently indoors, away from the distractions of Country
Country is relevant only to geography lessons, as a source of facts about landforms
Country acts as a teacher: knowledge is learned through relationships with land, kin and community
These knowledge systems are multimodal and relational; frameworks such as 8 Ways highlight story sharing, land links, and non-verbal and community links.
vce-psych34-atkinson-shiffrin-multi-stor: psych34a2-asm-1
In the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model of memory, which of the following is the correct order in which information flows when it is successfully retained for a long time?
Sensory memory, long-term memory, short-term memory
Long-term memory, short-term memory, sensory memory
Short-term memory, sensory memory, long-term memory
Sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory
Information passes from sensory memory (attention) to short-term memory and, through rehearsal, to long-term memory. Retrieval then returns information from LTM to STM.
psych34a2-asm-2
Which of the following best describes the capacity and duration of short-term memory according to the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?
Unlimited capacity and potentially permanent duration
About 7 ± 2 items and about 12 to 30 seconds without rehearsal
About 7 ± 2 items and several minutes without rehearsal
A few hundred items and about 3 to 4 seconds
STM holds about 5 to 9 items for approximately 12 to 30 seconds without rehearsal. Option D confuses STM with sensory memory duration.
psych34a2-asm-3
Brian looks at a street scene as he walks past. He can recall almost nothing about it a minute later, because he did not pay attention to most of it. This is best explained by
a lack of retrieval cues in long-term memory
failure of procedural memory
information being displaced from long-term memory
information in sensory memory decaying because it was not attended to
Unattended sensory information decays within a very short time (iconic memory under about a second, echoic 3 to 4 seconds) and does not transfer to STM.
psych34a2-asm-4

A researcher presents participants with a list of 20 words and then tests recall. People commonly recall the first few and last few words best. The better recall of the first words is typically explained by the Atkinson-Shiffrin model as
more rehearsal, so these words are more likely to be transferred to long-term memory
the words being stored in procedural memory
the last words displacing the first words from long-term memory
the words still being held in sensory memory
The primacy effect reflects greater rehearsal of early items, increasing the chance of transfer to LTM. The recency effect reflects items still in STM.
psych34a2-asm-5
Which of the following is a limitation of the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model?
It suggests that memory has more than one store
It describes sensory memory as having a very short duration
It treats short-term memory as a single store and does not explain how different types of long-term memory work or the role of processing beyond rehearsal
It proposes that information can be rehearsed
Critics note that STM is more than a passive store (see working memory) and that the model oversimplifies LTM and the importance of types of processing. A, B and D are features, not limitations.
psych34a2-asm-6
Distinguish between iconic memory and echoic memory, including the typical duration of each. (3 marks)

Iconic memory is the sensory memory for visual information; duration is a fraction of a second (about 0.2 to 0.4 seconds); echoic memory is the sensory memory for auditory information; duration about 3 to 4 seconds.
psych34a2-asm-7

Maya is trying to remember a phone number she has just been told. Using the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model, explain how she could ensure the number is stored for a long period of time, and what will most likely happen if she is interrupted straight after hearing it. (4 marks)

She must attend to the number so it moves from sensory memory to short-term memory (1); she needs to rehearse it (e.g. maintenance or elaborative rehearsal) so it is transferred to long-term memory (1 to 2 marks for explaining rehearsal and transfer to LTM); if interrupted, the number will not be rehearsed and will be lost from STM within about 12 to 30 seconds through decay or displacement, so it is not transferred to LTM (1).
psych34a2-asm-8
Describe how the serial position effect provides evidence for separate short-term and long-term memory stores. (3 marks)

Serial position effect: better recall of items at the start (primacy) and end (recency) of a list than the middle; primacy is explained by early items being rehearsed and transferred to LTM; recency is explained by the last items still being held in STM; the middle items are lost because they are displaced from STM before they are rehearsed enough to enter LTM, which supports the existence of two stores.
vce-psych34-as-c1
You were not listening, but a second after a friend asks a question you can 'replay' it and answer. Which memory store made this possible?
Iconic sensory memory, which holds images for about 0.2–0.4 seconds
Long-term memory, because it has unlimited capacity
Echoic sensory memory, which holds sounds for about 3–4 seconds
Short-term memory, because it lasts 18–30 seconds without attention
Auditory information lingers in echoic memory briefly; attending to it then transfers it to short-term memory.
vce-psych34-explicit-and-implicit-memory: psych34a2-eim-1
Which of the following is an example of implicit memory?
Recalling the date of your last birthday party
Naming the capital city of France
Riding a bike without consciously thinking about each movement
Describing the plot of a film you saw last week
Riding a bike is procedural (implicit) memory: it is expressed through performance without conscious recall. A and D are episodic and B is semantic, all explicit.
psych34a2-eim-2
Semantic memory is best described as
memory of personal experiences tied to a particular time and place
memory of general facts and knowledge about the world
memory of skills and habits
memory of conditioned emotional responses
Semantic memory stores general knowledge and facts (a type of explicit memory). Option A describes episodic memory.
psych34a2-eim-3

A participant is shown a series of words and later asked to complete word fragments such as 'ch_ir'. They are more likely to complete fragments with previously seen words, but do not remember seeing the list. This is evidence of
implicit memory, because past experience influenced performance without conscious recollection
episodic memory, because the words were seen in a specific place
the serial position effect
explicit memory, because they recalled the words
Priming-type effects show that prior exposure influences performance without conscious recall, indicating implicit memory.
psych34a2-eim-4
Which of the following correctly matches a type of memory with an example?
Classically conditioned response: feeling anxious when you hear a dentist's drill
Semantic memory: recalling what you ate for breakfast yesterday
Episodic memory: knowing how to tie shoelaces
Procedural memory: remembering your graduation day
An emotional response learned through classical conditioning is stored implicitly. Tying shoelaces is procedural, graduation day is episodic and breakfast yesterday is episodic.
psych34a2-eim-5
Which statement correctly distinguishes explicit memory from implicit memory?
Explicit memory is unconscious and implicit memory is conscious
Explicit memory requires conscious recall and can be declared; implicit memory influences behaviour without conscious awareness
Explicit memory is stored only in the cerebellum
Implicit memory includes only episodic memory
Explicit (declarative) memory involves conscious retrieval; implicit (non-declarative) memory is expressed through behaviour without conscious effort.
psych34a2-eim-6
Name the two types of explicit memory and give one example of each. (4 marks)

Episodic memory (1) with a suitable example, e.g. remembering your 10th birthday party or what you did yesterday (1); semantic memory (1) with a suitable example, e.g. knowing that Canberra is the capital of Australia (1).
psych34a2-eim-7

Jamal learnt to play the piano as a child and has not played for 20 years. He sits at a piano and finds his fingers move through a familiar piece, but he cannot recall where or when he learnt it. Identify the types of memory shown in this scenario, and justify each choice. (4 marks)

Procedural (implicit) memory (1) because he can perform the skill without conscious recall of how (1); episodic (explicit) memory failure/absence (1) because he cannot consciously recall the specific time and place of the learning (1). (Also acceptable: contrast between implicit retained and explicit lost.)
psych34a2-eim-8
Explain why a person who has lost the ability to form new explicit memories may still be able to learn a new motor skill. (3 marks)

Explicit and implicit memories are stored and processed separately, involving different brain regions; the person's explicit memory system (e.g. hippocampus) is damaged, preventing formation of new conscious memories; implicit procedural memory (e.g. involving the cerebellum) remains intact so the skill improves with practice even though they cannot recall the practice sessions.
vce-psych34-ei-c1
Sara feels anxious every time she sits in a dentist's waiting room, though she cannot recall any bad experience there. This anxiety is an example of:
Episodic memory
Semantic memory
Explicit memory, because she is aware of the feeling
Implicit memory (classically conditioned)
Classically conditioned responses are implicit: they are expressed without conscious recall of the learning event.
vce-psych34-brain-regions-in-memory: psych34a2-brm-1
Which brain region is primarily involved in the consolidation of new explicit memories?
Brainstem
Cerebellum
Hippocampus
Amygdala

The hippocampus is critical for consolidating explicit memories, which are then stored in the neocortex. The cerebellum is involved in implicit memories such as motor skills and classically conditioned responses.
psych34a2-brm-2
The amygdala's role in memory is best described as
forming procedural memories for movement
attaching emotional significance to memories, especially fear-related, and enhancing their consolidation
short-term storage of visual information
storing semantic memories permanently
The amygdala is involved in the emotional components of memory and strengthens memories of emotionally charged events. Procedural memory involves the cerebellum.
psych34a2-brm-3

After surgery to remove both hippocampi, a patient can still learn to trace shapes in a mirror, with improved performance over days, but cannot remember doing the task. Which conclusion is best supported?
Implicit memory is lost when the hippocampus is removed
Procedural memory depends on the hippocampus
Explicit memory formation depends on the hippocampus, while procedural learning does not
The amygdala is responsible for mirror tracing
Improved skill without recall shows intact implicit procedural memory and impaired formation of explicit memory, which depends on the hippocampus.
psych34a2-brm-4
Which of the following correctly matches a brain region with its role in memory?
Neocortex: long-term storage of explicit memories
Cerebellum: consolidation of episodic memories
Hippocampus: storage of classically conditioned responses
Amygdala: formation of procedural memories
The neocortex is where explicit memories are ultimately stored, with different regions storing different aspects. The cerebellum is involved in implicit memories, not episodic consolidation.
psych34a2-brm-5

A person is attacked by a dog and later feels intense fear and an elevated heart rate whenever they hear barking, even though they cannot recall details of the attack. Which brain region is most likely involved in this emotional response?
Prefrontal cortex only
Broca's area
Hippocampus
Amygdala
The amygdala processes and stores emotional (fear) responses, which can occur without explicit recall. The hippocampus is more involved in explicit details.
psych34a2-brm-6
Describe the roles of the hippocampus and the cerebellum in memory. (3 marks)

Hippocampus: involved in the encoding and consolidation of new explicit (episodic and semantic) memories, which are then stored in the neocortex (1 to 2 marks); cerebellum: involved in the formation and storage of implicit memories such as procedural memory (motor skills) and classically conditioned responses (1 mark).
psych34a2-brm-7

A man known as patient K has damage to his hippocampus following an accident. He can remember events from his childhood but cannot recall conversations from earlier the same day. He can learn a new sport with practice. Using your knowledge of brain regions in memory, explain these observations. (4 marks)

Childhood memories were already consolidated and are stored in the neocortex, so remain accessible (1); damaged hippocampus prevents consolidation of new explicit (episodic) memories, so recent conversations are not recalled (1 to 2); learning a sport is implicit procedural memory, involving the cerebellum, which is intact (1).
psych34a2-brm-8
Explain how the amygdala and the hippocampus work together when a person forms a memory of a frightening event. (3 marks)

The hippocampus encodes and consolidates the explicit details of the event, such as where and when it happened (1); the amygdala processes the emotional significance (fear) and enhances the strength of consolidation (1); together the memory is stronger and more vivid, with emotional response and factual details linked (1).
vce-psych34-br-c1
After surgery removing much of his hippocampi, a patient improved at a mirror-drawing task over several days but never remembered practising it. This suggests that:
The hippocampus is needed to consolidate explicit memories, while procedural skills rely on other regions
The hippocampus stores all long-term memories, so his skills must have come from short-term memory
The cerebellum consolidates episodic memories, so he should have remembered the practice sessions
Procedural memories are stored in the amygdala, which also holds his memories of the sessions
His implicit (procedural) learning was intact but he could not form new explicit memories of the sessions.
vce-psych34-autobiographical-memory-and-: psych34a2-ama-1
Autobiographical memory is best described as
memory for facts learnt in school
memory of personal life experiences and personal knowledge about oneself
memory for skills and habits
memory that is only formed in childhood
Autobiographical memory is memory of one's own life, combining episodic memories of events and semantic knowledge about oneself. Option A describes semantic memory in general.
psych34a2-ama-2
Aphantasia is best described as
an inability to recognise faces
a condition in which a person cannot voluntarily form mental images
a complete loss of long-term memory
a form of amnesia caused by damage to the amygdala
Aphantasia is the absence or severe reduction of voluntary visual mental imagery. Face blindness is prosopagnosia.
psych34a2-ama-3
Compared with people who experience typical mental imagery, people with aphantasia are most likely to report that their autobiographical memories
contain more visual details
are limited to procedural memories
are not available at all
contain fewer sensory and visual details, although they may still recall facts about the events
Research shows people with aphantasia often report autobiographical memories that lack vivid sensory, especially visual, detail, but they retain factual information about the events.
psych34a2-ama-4

A researcher asks a person to 'picture your breakfast table this morning' and then describe it. The person says they know what was there (cereal, a glass of juice) but 'see nothing at all in my mind'. This is most consistent with
aphantasia
synaesthesia
prosopagnosia
amnesia
Knowing the facts without being able to visualise suggests aphantasia, not a memory loss.
psych34a2-ama-5
Which of the following is an appropriate conclusion about aphantasia and memory from this type of evidence?
People with aphantasia have better semantic than procedural memory
People with aphantasia cannot form episodic memories
Visual imagery may enrich the vividness of recalled episodes but is not required to remember what happened
Aphantasia is caused by damage to the cerebellum
Evidence suggests aphantasia affects the sensory richness of recollection but not necessarily the ability to recall events. The cause is not established as cerebellar damage.
psych34a2-ama-6
Outline what is meant by autobiographical memory and name the two types of explicit memory it draws on. (3 marks)

Autobiographical memory is memory of events and information about one's own life (1); it draws on episodic memory (personal events and experiences) (1) and semantic memory (personal facts, e.g. where you went to school) (1).
psych34a2-ama-7

A study compares two groups on a task that asks participants to describe a past event, such as their last holiday, in as much detail as possible. Group A reports vivid mental imagery. Group B reports aphantasia. Group B gives fewer sensory details, but the number of factual details is similar across groups. Explain what these results suggest about the role of imagery in autobiographical memory. (3 marks)

Imagery contributes to the vividness and sensory richness of recalled events (1); factual (semantic/episodic) information can be retrieved without imagery (1); so imagery is not necessary for the retrieval of autobiographical information, but it influences the quality or detail of recollection (1).
psych34a2-ama-8
Identify one limitation of using self-report to investigate aphantasia, and suggest how a researcher could address it. (3 marks)

Limitation (1): imagery is subjective, so people may differ in how they interpret or rate vividness, so responses may be unreliable or biased; address (up to 2): use objective measures in addition, such as performance on tasks requiring imagery, physiological responses or comparing with brain imaging, or use standardised scales such as a validated vividness questionnaire and compare across a large sample.
vce-psych34-am-c1
People with aphantasia often report less vivid autobiographical memories. The best explanation is that:
They have no long-term memory, so they cannot store any events from their lives
They cannot voluntarily form mental images, which help people re-experience past events
Their hippocampus has been removed, so new memories cannot be consolidated
They cannot remember any facts about themselves, such as where they grew up
Aphantasia affects mental imagery, not general memory. Semantic knowledge about their lives is usually intact.
vce-psych34-alzheimers-disease: psych34a2-alz-1
Alzheimer's disease is best described as
a disorder caused by a single traumatic head injury
a condition affecting only procedural memory
a temporary memory loss caused by sleep deprivation
a progressive neurodegenerative disease resulting in loss of neurons and increasing memory and cognitive impairment
Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease. It typically affects explicit memory early, not procedural memory.
psych34a2-alz-2
Which of the following brain changes is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease?
An increase in the number of neurons in the hippocampus
Build-up of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, with neuron loss
Complete destruction of the cerebellum
Enlargement of the amygdala
Beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles lead to neuron death and brain atrophy.
psych34a2-alz-3
Which of the following is most likely to be one of the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer's disease?
Inability to recognise close family members
Loss of procedural memory for riding a bike
Loss of the ability to walk
Difficulty forming new episodic memories, such as forgetting recent conversations
The hippocampus is affected early, so difficulty forming new explicit memories appears first. Loss of recognition of family and mobility occurs later.
psych34a2-alz-4
Why might a person with advanced Alzheimer's disease still be able to play a piece on the piano they learnt many years ago?
Procedural memory depends on regions such as the cerebellum that are affected later than the hippocampus and neocortex
Piano playing relies on semantic memory only
Alzheimer's disease does not affect long-term memories
The hippocampus is spared until the final stage
Implicit procedural memories are more resistant, as they rely on regions less affected early in the disease. A is incorrect since the hippocampus is affected early.
psych34a2-alz-5
As Alzheimer's disease progresses, the loss of neurons in the neocortex is most likely to result in
no changes to behaviour or personality
improved retrieval of semantic memories
decline in language, reasoning and stored explicit memories
improved attention
Neocortical neuron loss affects stored explicit memories and cognitive functions such as language, reasoning and judgement, and can lead to personality changes.
psych34a2-alz-6
Describe two physical changes in the brain associated with Alzheimer's disease. (2 marks)

Any two: formation of amyloid plaques between neurons (1); neurofibrillary tangles of tau protein within neurons (1); loss of neurons and synapses (1); shrinkage (atrophy) of regions such as the hippocampus and neocortex (1); reduced levels of neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine (1).
psych34a2-alz-7

Margaret, aged 72, has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Her family notes that she often repeats questions and forgets recent events but can still make a cup of tea and recall her wedding day in detail. Using knowledge of memory, explain these observations. (4 marks)

Damage to the hippocampus affects consolidation of new explicit memories, so recent events and repeated questions are forgotten (1 to 2); making tea is a procedural (implicit) memory, which is stored in regions such as the cerebellum that are affected later (1); her wedding day is an old, consolidated episodic memory stored in the neocortex, which is initially less affected (1).
psych34a2-alz-8
Explain how the progression of Alzheimer's disease can have implications for a person's daily functioning and for their family. (3 marks)

As neurons are lost, memory, language and reasoning decline, leading to difficulty with daily tasks such as managing money, cooking or self-care, and eventually needing full-time care (1 to 2); family members may experience emotional, financial and physical strain as carers and may grieve as the person's personality and ability to recognise them changes (1).
vce-psych34-ad-c1
Which pairing about Alzheimer's disease is correct?
Amyloid plaques form inside neurons; tau tangles form between neurons
Both form only in the cerebellum
Amyloid plaques form between neurons; neurofibrillary tangles of tau form inside neurons
Tangles are made of GABA; plaques are made of glutamate
Beta-amyloid builds up outside neurons and tau tangles inside them, contributing to neuron death, especially in the hippocampus early on.
vce-psych34-mnemonics: psych34a2-mne-1
A student remembers the order of the planets by using the sentence 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles'. This mnemonic is an example of
an acrostic
the method of loci
chunking
an acronym
An acrostic uses the first letters of words to form a new sentence. An acronym forms a single word (e.g. ROYGBIV is an acronym-style device).
psych34a2-mne-2
Which of the following is an example of the method of loci?
Repeating a list of words over and over
Remembering a phone number as three groups of digits
Imagining placing each item on a shopping list at a distinct location along a familiar route through your house
Using the word HOMES to remember the Great Lakes
The method of loci associates items with locations on a familiar route. A is chunking, C is an acronym and D is maintenance rehearsal.
psych34a2-mne-3
A person remembers the 10-digit number 0412345678 as 0412 345 678. This strategy is best described as
the method of loci
an acrostic
a classically conditioned response
chunking
Chunking groups items into meaningful units, effectively increasing the amount of information held in short-term memory.
psych34a2-mne-4
Why are mnemonics effective in improving memory?
They increase the duration of sensory memory
They remove the need for attention
They erase irrelevant information from long-term memory
They organise information and link it to existing knowledge or cues, which improves encoding and retrieval
Mnemonics provide structure and retrieval cues by linking new information to familiar patterns, images or places.
psych34a2-mne-5
A student is asked to remember the following rainbow colours in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. She uses ROY G. BIV. This is an example of
an acrostic
an acronym
the method of loci
the serial position effect
An acronym uses the initial letters of items to form a new word or abbreviation.
psych34a2-mne-6
Define a mnemonic and give one example of a mnemonic device. (2 marks)

A mnemonic is a memory aid or technique used to improve encoding and retrieval of information, often by organising it or linking it to something familiar (1); example: acronym, acrostic, method of loci or chunking, with a suitable example (1).
psych34a2-mne-7
Sam needs to memorise a list of 12 items for a presentation. Describe how Sam could use the method of loci to do this and explain why it may help recall. (4 marks)

Choose a familiar route or place, e.g. walking through a house (1); create a vivid image of each item and place it in a distinct location along the route in order (1 to 2); at recall, mentally walk the route and retrieve each item from its location (1); helps because locations provide retrieval cues and a sequence, and vivid imagery adds elaboration (1).
psych34a2-mne-8
Explain how chunking can overcome the limited capacity of short-term memory. (3 marks)

STM has a limited capacity of about 7 ± 2 items (1); chunking groups individual items into larger meaningful units (1); each chunk counts as one item, so more information can be held in STM and later transferred to LTM (1).
vce-psych34-mn-c1
Why are Songlines an effective mnemonic for storing large amounts of knowledge in oral cultures?
They use the first letter of each word as a written cue, in the same way as an acronym or acrostic
They link knowledge to places on Country through story, song and movement, giving many retrieval cues
They work only for numbers and dates, which are linked to the rhythm of each song
They rely on writing the information down in sequence before it is sung aloud
Songlines combine the advantages of the method of loci (place-based cues) with narrative, music and repetition.
vce-psych34-consciousness-and-measuring-: psych34a2-cms-1
Consciousness is best defined as
the ability to control all bodily processes
the level of awareness a person has of their internal states and external environment
the same as being awake
a state that can only be measured by observation
