pieces.answer: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Low GABA activity means less inhibition of neural firing, so the stress response is triggered more easily and anxiety is heightened.

steps.working: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that reduces the likelihood of postsynaptic neurons firing.
If GABA is not working effectively, neurons fire more readily, contributing to excessive anxiety and fear responses.

pieces.mistake: Calling GABA an excitatory neurotransmitter. Glutamate is the main excitatory one.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Describe how systematic desensitisation could be used to treat Priya's phobia.
pieces.answer: Priya learns relaxation techniques and builds a fear hierarchy, then is gradually exposed to each step (from a picture of a dog to touching a calm dog) while staying relaxed, until the fear response is replaced.

steps.working: Priya is taught relaxation techniques and creates a fear hierarchy from least to most anxiety-provoking situations involving dogs.
She is exposed to each step gradually while relaxed, moving up only when calm, so relaxation replaces fear (reciprocal inhibition).

pieces.mistake: Describing flooding, where she would be exposed to the most feared situation at once.

X.title: Night shifts and sleep
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Psychology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Sam is a nurse who works a run of night shifts, sleeping during the day.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain how working night shifts disrupts Sam's circadian rhythm.
pieces.answer: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is entrained to daylight. Sam is awake at night and tries to sleep in daylight, so light exposure suppresses melatonin when he needs to sleep, and his body clock is misaligned with his schedule.

steps.working: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) uses light as a zeitgeber to set the timing of the sleep–wake cycle.
Sam's exposure to daylight when he needs to sleep suppresses melatonin release, so his circadian rhythm is out of step with his sleep schedule.

pieces.mistake: Saying shift work stops melatonin being produced altogether. It shifts when melatonin is released.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Sam has been awake for 17 hours by the end of a shift. Compare his likely performance with a blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
pieces.answer: 17 hours awake is roughly equivalent to a BAC of 0.05; 24 hours awake is roughly equivalent to 0.10.

steps.working: About 17 hours of sustained wakefulness produces impairment similar to a BAC of 0.05.
Impairment keeps rising: about 24 hours awake is similar to a BAC of 0.10.

pieces.mistake: Giving the values the wrong way round. The longer awake, the higher the equivalent BAC.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Describe how bright light therapy could help Sam adjust to night shifts.
pieces.answer: Exposure to bright artificial light at chosen times (for example at the start of his shift) helps shift the SCN's timing, delaying melatonin release so that he is alert at night and sleepy in the day.

steps.working: Sam is exposed to bright artificial light for a set time at a specific point in his schedule.
The light acts on the SCN to shift the circadian rhythm and the timing of melatonin release, realigning it with his work schedule.

pieces.mistake: Saying the light makes him tired. Bright light promotes alertness; its timing shifts the rhythm.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Which type of sleep dominates the first half of a typical night, and which dominates the second half?
pieces.answer: Deep NREM sleep (stage 3) dominates the first half; REM sleep periods become longer in the second half.

steps.working: First half: more deep NREM sleep (stage 3).
Second half: REM periods lengthen and dominate.

pieces.mistake: Reversing them. REM periods are short early in the night and lengthen towards morning.

pieces.text: A researcher measured the reaction times of 12 nurses after a night shift and again after a day shift.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Name the experimental design and give one advantage of using it in this study.
pieces.answer: Within-subjects (repeated measures) design; each nurse is compared with themselves, which controls participant-related extraneous variables such as natural reaction speed.

steps.working: Within-subjects design: every nurse is tested in both conditions.
Advantage: it controls participant differences (such as natural reaction speed), so differences are more likely due to the shift type; it also needs fewer participants.

pieces.mistake: Naming a between-subjects design. The same nurses are tested twice.

X.title: Challenge: exam stress and sleep
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Psychology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Ava is a Year 12 student. In the month before her exams she thinks, 'If I fail, I won't get into my course.' She then decides she has no time to ask her teachers for help. She studies on her laptop until 1 am most nights and has to wake at 6:30 am.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Identify Ava's primary and secondary appraisals using the transactional model of stress and coping.
pieces.answer: Primary: stressful (threat), as she anticipates future harm (failing). Secondary: she judges her coping resources as inadequate (no time for help).

steps.working: Primary appraisal: stressful, threat (potential future harm).
Secondary appraisal: evaluation of coping resources, judged insufficient.

pieces.mistake: Labelling it a challenge appraisal. She focuses on potential harm, not gain.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain how cortisol released over several weeks could affect Ava.
pieces.answer: Cortisol keeps energy available and resistance above normal, but prolonged release suppresses the immune system, making illness more likely.

steps.working: Cortisol maintains raised energy and alertness (resistance stage).
Prolonged cortisol suppresses immune function.

pieces.mistake: Confusing cortisol with adrenaline, which acts within seconds.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain how screen use until 1 am is likely to affect when Ava falls asleep.
pieces.answer: Blue light from the screen is a zeitgeber that signals the SCN to suppress melatonin, so sleep onset is delayed beyond her already later adolescent sleep phase.

steps.working: Light acts on the SCN and suppresses melatonin.
Sleep onset is delayed, adding to the adolescent sleep–wake shift.

pieces.mistake: Saying screens make melatonin go up.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Ava gets about 5.5 hours of sleep a night. Describe one likely affective and one likely cognitive effect of this partial sleep deprivation.
pieces.answer: Affective: irritability or poorer emotional regulation. Cognitive: poorer concentration, slower thinking or worse decisions.

steps.working: A correct affective effect.
A correct cognitive effect.

pieces.mistake: Describing behavioural effects only (such as yawning).

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Recommend one approach coping strategy for Ava and explain why it would suit her situation better than avoidance.
pieces.answer: Making a study plan and asking teachers for help: it deals directly with the stressor, reducing the threat, whereas avoidance gives short-term relief but leaves the problem.

steps.working: A valid approach strategy linked to her stressor.
Explains why it is more effective than avoidance in this context.

pieces.mistake: Recommending exercise without explaining how it suits her situation.

X.title: Challenge: testing a phobia treatment
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Psychology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Researchers recruited 30 adults with a specific phobia of spiders. Participants were randomly allocated to two groups. Group A received six sessions of systematic desensitisation; Group B received six sessions of psychoeducation only. Each participant rated their anxiety (0 = none, 10 = extreme) when shown a live spider in a sealed tank before and after treatment.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Write a hypothesis for this study.
pieces.answer: Adults with a spider phobia who receive systematic desensitisation will show a greater decrease in anxiety rating when shown a live spider than those who receive psychoeducation only.

steps.working: Names the IV (type of treatment) and the DV (change in anxiety rating).
Is directional and refers to the population.

pieces.mistake: Writing a question rather than a testable prediction.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Identify the experimental design and give one advantage of it for this study.
pieces.answer: Between-subjects design; there are no order effects, since each participant receives only one treatment.

steps.working: Between-subjects (independent groups).
A valid advantage, such as no order effects or less time needed per participant.

pieces.mistake: Calling it within-subjects because anxiety was measured twice.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Calculate the change in mean anxiety for each group and state a conclusion.
pieces.answer: A fell by 5.1; B fell by 1.5. Systematic desensitisation appears more effective than psychoeducation alone, which supports the hypothesis for this sample.

steps.working: Correct changes: 5.1 and 1.5.
A conclusion limited to the sample, linked to the hypothesis.

pieces.mistake: Claiming the treatment is proven to work for everyone.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain how systematic desensitisation reduces the fear response.
pieces.answer: The person learns relaxation, then is gradually exposed to a fear hierarchy while relaxed. Relaxation is incompatible with fear, so the conditioned fear response is replaced (counterconditioning) and extinguished.

steps.working: Relaxation training plus gradual exposure through a fear hierarchy.
Relaxation replaces the conditioned fear response.

pieces.mistake: Describing flooding (immediate full exposure).

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Identify one ethical guideline the researchers must follow, and explain why it matters in this study.
pieces.answer: Withdrawal rights: being shown a spider could be very distressing, so participants must be able to stop at any time without penalty.

steps.working: Names a relevant guideline.
Explains its importance in this study.

pieces.mistake: Naming a guideline without linking it to the phobia study.
